steps.explanationAfterStep: Protonation turns methoxide, a very poor leaving group, into methanol, a good one.

The ring oxygen pushes methanol out, giving the oxocarbenium ion. A ring-oxygen lone pair anti-periplanar to the breaking C–O bond is ideally placed: the same n → σ* overlap that makes the axial OMe group more stable than you would expect (the anomeric effect) is what helps it leave.
Water adds to the planar oxocarbenium ion from either face, so both anomers of the hemiacetal form; the axial one is again favoured by the anomeric effect. The app does not check stereochemistry yet.
H₃O⁺ is returned. The hemiacetal is in equilibrium with the open-chain hydroxy aldehyde, just as glucose is with its open form.

title: Acid hydrolysis of a glycoside model
subtitle: The anomeric effect: a ring oxygen lone pair pushes the leaving group out
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 31 (Saturated heterocycles and stereoelectronics)
Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 11 (Nucleophilic substitution at C=O with loss of carbonyl oxygen)

reactants.caption: 2-methoxytetrahydropyran (an acetal; OMe mostly axial) + dilute HCl
hintTiers: Acetals are stable to base but not to acid. Which oxygen should be protonated so that a neutral molecule can leave?
The methoxy oxygen takes a proton from H₃O⁺; that O–H bonding pair stays on water. Two arrows.
Methoxy oxygen lone pair → new O–H bond to a proton of H₃O⁺; that O–H bond → lone pair on water's oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: Dilute acid hydrolyses the acetal. Start with the acid.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Protonating the ring oxygen also happens, and would open the ring. The main route protonates the methoxy oxygen, so that methanol leaves and the ring stays.
Water is too weak a nucleophile to displace methoxide directly. Acid first, then the ring oxygen pushes methanol out.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right oxygen. Where does the O–H bonding pair of H₃O⁺ go?

hemiacetal.caption: tetrahydropyran-2-ol (a hemiacetal, in equilibrium with 5-hydroxypentanal) + methanol + H₃O⁺, returned

oxocarbenium.caption: oxocarbenium ion + methanol
hintTiers: The positive charge is shared by the ring oxygen and the anomeric carbon. Where does water attack?
A water oxygen bonds to the anomeric carbon, and the C=O⁺ π pair returns to the ring oxygen. Two arrows.
Water oxygen lone pair → new O–C bond to the anomeric carbon; C=O⁺ π bond → lone pair on the ring oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The ring oxygen keeps its octet, as in all oxocarbenium ions: the carbon is where a nucleophile bonds.
Methanol could add back, but it is a minor species in dilute aqueous acid: water, in huge excess, wins.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: water attacks the anomeric carbon. Move the C=O⁺ π pair.

protonated-acetal.caption: acetal protonated on the methoxy oxygen
hintTiers: Which lone pair can push methanol out? It is best placed when it lies anti-periplanar to the breaking C–O bond.
A ring-oxygen lone pair forms a C=O⁺ π bond as the C–O bond to the protonated methoxy group breaks. Two arrows.
Ring oxygen lone pair → π bond to the anomeric carbon (the carbon between the two oxygens); C–O bond to the methoxy oxygen → lone pair on that oxygen.
protonated-acetal.learnerPrompt: Methanol leaves, helped by the ring oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: An SN2 at an acetal carbon is slow: the ring oxygen makes an SN1 route much easier. Let methanol leave first.
That gives the proton back to water. Methanol is now a good leaving group: let it go.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: methanol leaves. Which lone pair fills the gap at the anomeric carbon?

protonated-hemiacetal.caption: protonated hemiacetal
hintTiers: The new OH₂⁺ group is very acidic. Which base is at hand?
Another water molecule takes a proton from the OH₂⁺ group. Two arrows.
Water lone pair → new O–H bond to a proton of the OH₂⁺ group; that O–H bond → lone pair on its oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing water again goes back to the oxocarbenium ion. Deprotonate instead.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: water takes the proton. Where does the O–H bonding pair go?

mechanismSummary: 2-Methoxytetrahydropyran is a model of a methyl glycoside: an acetal with one oxygen in the ring. Its OMe group prefers the axial position (the anomeric effect): a lone pair of the ring oxygen lies anti-periplanar to the C–OMe bond and feeds into its σ* orbital. In dilute acid the methoxy oxygen is protonated, and the ring oxygen pushes methanol out, giving an oxocarbenium ion; the same anti-periplanar lone pair makes this easy. Water adds to the cation and loses a proton, giving the hemiacetal (a lactol), which is in equilibrium with 5-hydroxypentanal. Glucosides and other glycosides are hydrolysed the same way. The app does not check stereochemistry yet, so the axial preference is not drawn.
